The full write-up is in `docs/research/qwen-wan-shortlist-postmortem.md`.

## Core finding

A good Qwen endpoint is not necessarily a good Wan endpoint.

Humans see an attractive second image and imagine a plausible history. Wan must actually render that history. It receives no smoke-particle correspondence, motion vectors, or object masks—only two stills and text.

Each endpoint therefore implied different physics:

- S08: attraction into a sink
- S18: flow plus object materialization
- S36: disappearance followed by re-emission
- S42: typography transformed into smoke
- S54: one locally translated plume

The Wan prompt was identical. The endpoint differences dictated the behavior.

## S08 — The vortex

![S08 progression](/tmp/comfyui-images/smoke_wan_s08_contact.png)

The endpoint looked good because it created the strongest full-width smoke composition. It clearly communicated force and direction while retaining plausible curl texture.

But it did not translate a fixed amount of smoke. It retained smoke at the left while adding a connected path across the frame. Wan interpreted that topology as:

```text
stationary source + connected smoke path + increasing destination density

That resembles suction or convergence more than ambient drift.

Your vacuum observation changes the interpretation substantially. In a vacuum-cleaner advertisement, the vortex may be the strongest concept of all. Wan saw a large appliance whose semantic purpose is suction and found a coherent explanation for the image delta: all the room’s smoke is being pulled into an attractor.

For uniform atmospheric drift, S08 failed. For intentional vacuum suction, it may have accidentally succeeded.

The lesson: uncleared source smoke plus a long connected destination plume implies emission or attraction. If we embrace suction, every smoke region should bend toward the nozzle and visibly clear its source area.

S18 — Good flow, catastrophic scene contamination

S18 proves that the smoke itself can have excellent correspondence. Wan found a plausible flowing path rather than merely dissolving one cloud and growing another.

Unfortunately, Qwen also duplicated solid scene content: a miniature throne and vacuum-like form appeared above the original throne.

At gallery scale, attention naturally goes to the smoke, so that error is easy to overlook. During video generation it becomes impossible to miss. Wan must reach the duplicated-object endpoint, so the extra chair grows into existence.

Smoke becomes a convenient material from which to manifest it.

The likely Qwen failure is latent entanglement: the smoke overlapped the throne, so the “transparent layer” metaphor selected semantic content behind the smoke as well as the smoke itself.

The lesson: a tiny endpoint object error becomes a full animated apparition. Before passing an endpoint to Wan, we need to reject changes in object count, silhouettes, text regions, throne geometry, vacuum position, and other high-contrast structures.

Excellent smoke motion cannot rescue a corrupted scene graph.

S36 — Attractive composition, wrong history

S36 looked good because the final smoke masses were dramatic and compositionally balanced. The result reads as an intentional cinematic still.

But its source and destination smoke regions have weak correspondence. Wan cannot trace one plume through overlapping positions. It instead takes a cheaper route:

original smoke diminishes
→ room becomes relatively clear
→ new smoke condenses around the throne

That produces the impression that smoke flows inward and then outward again.

This is not continuous translation. It is fade-out followed by re-emission. The endpoint’s disjoint smoke topology effectively describes an oscillation, regardless of the prompt’s word “continuous.”

Again, the vacuum could provide a narrative excuse: perhaps suction starts, clears the room, then stops and allows smoke to rebound. But that would need to be an intentional pulse or oscillation with a visible cause.

The lesson: when start and endpoint smoke masks do not overlap enough, Wan prefers disappearance/reappearance. Translation needs spatial overlap or an intermediate keyframe.

S42 — The neon sign’s soul

S42 looked dynamic because it had a strong horizontal smoke trajectory. At thumbnail size, that dominates perception.

But the endpoint also:

  • duplicated the neon title;
  • moved it above the television;
  • placed “CLOSED” on the television;
  • altered the original sign’s state; and
  • overlapped smoke with luminous letter strokes.

Wan had to transform the original typography into that endpoint typography. Smoke and neon are visually compatible materials: both are bright, curved, semi-transparent shapes against black.

So Wan found an economical transition: extract the glowing letters, stretch them, and turn them into smoke-like material. Your “sucking out the soul” description is exactly what the endpoint pair requests visually.

The text prompt saying “hold typography fixed” cannot override an endpoint where typography is visibly different. Wan must reach the supplied last frame.

The lesson: text mutation is an automatic rejection condition. Correct spelling is not enough—we must also verify text count, bounding boxes, positions, and whether any lettering appeared on the television or elsewhere.

S54 — The best local solution, not a global one

S54 worked because it presented Wan with the lowest-complexity explanation:

  • objects remained stable;
  • text remained stable;
  • the camera and composition remained stable;
  • one gray plume had recognizable correspondence; and
  • that plume occupied overlapping, progressively displaced positions.

Wan could animate one local advection without inventing chairs, moving signs, or changing scene semantics.

But your “trees versus forest” diagnosis is correct. S54 only advanced the obvious left plume. The upper haze, middle-ground wisps, and much of the pink smoke remained nearly identical between endpoints.

If a smoke region is identical in both endpoint images, moving it continuously would create a conflict: it would have to move during the clip and return to its original position before the final frame. Wan takes the cheaper path and leaves it static.

The prompt may say “all smoke moves,” but the endpoint pair says “only this plume moves.” The endpoint wins.

The lesson: global atmospheric motion requires a global atmospheric endpoint. Every region intended to move must visibly advance:

  1. left gray plume;
  2. upper-center haze;
  3. middle-ground wisps;
  4. pink smoke around the sign;
  5. diffuse ceiling haze.

They must all share either one rightward vector field or one converging suction field.

What we actually learned

The five outputs are not five versions of the same movement. They encode five different physical models:

  • S08: smoke converges into an attractor.
  • S18: smoke advects while a scene object materializes.
  • S36: smoke disappears and is emitted elsewhere.
  • S42: glowing semantic content morphs into smoke.
  • S54: one plume advects while the remaining atmosphere is anchored.

The “great second image” looked good because composition and implied motion were convincing. It ultimately failed whenever it did not unambiguously answer:

  • What exact material moved?
  • Where did every part originate?
  • Where did every part end?
  • Did the source location clear?
  • Did the plume remain one connected material?
  • Did every locked object remain identical?
  • Did all smoke regions follow the same physics?

S54 answered those questions for one plume. It did not answer them for the entire room.

The creative decision

We now have two valid directions.

Uniform ambient drift: Start from S54, but visibly advance every smoke region rightward in the endpoint.

Intentional vacuum suction: Build on S08 and make every smoke region curve toward the nozzle, with source regions clearing and density increasing only near the vacuum.

The suction concept may be more narratively compelling because it turns the vacuum from a static prop into the cause of the entire animation.

We wouldn’t trust an LLM saying “this plan is good.” It has to pass automatic gates.

Before Qwen:
- Every visible object/material is either locked or assigned to a track.
- Every change is a concrete still-state, not “heavier” or “more dramatic.”
- Every new destination state has a visible source/correspondence.
- No text, camera, object-count, or material contradiction.
- The critic must be able to state one plausible Wan interpretation for each frame pair.

Any failure escalates automatically to local Qwen 27B.

After each actual Qwen frame:
- A local vision QA compares previous frame + generated frame + approved contract.
- It checks scene/text preservation, required delta, material continuity, source clearance/destination occupancy, and whether the pair is Wan-safe.
- Critical failure stops the sequence; ordinary failure gets a targeted repair/retry, then Qwen 27B escalation. It never proceeds to Wan or publishes a “least bad” result.

After Wan:
- Sample first/middle/last frames and automatically reject camera drift, object/text morphing, or a freeze/restart signature.

So “good” becomes: all hard invariants pass, endpoint QA passes, and Wan QA passes—not a human judgement or model confidence.

## Result

No workflow is a true multi-source image-to-video, start/end-frame, keyframe interpolation, or continuity workflow. The only genuine video candidates are single-image Wan 2.2 I2V workflows.

### 1. `the local vault/ComfyUI-Shared/user/default/workflows/hearmeman-wan22-i2v.json`

Best candidate, but still single-image I2V.

- `LoadImage` — ID `img`
  - Loads `nsfw_edit_00050_.png`.
- `ImageScaleToTotalPixels` — ID `resize`
- `WanImageToVideo` — ID `i2v`
  - Its only image input is `start_image`.
  - Receives the resized image through link `29`.
  - Produces a video latent using text conditioning plus the single source image.
- High-noise path:
  - `UnetLoaderGGUF` — `hn_load`
  - `LoraLoaderModelOnly` — `hn_lora`
  - `ModelSamplingSD3` — `hn_ms`
  - `KSamplerAdvanced` — `hn_ks`
- Low-noise path:
  - `UnetLoaderGGUF` — `ln_load`
  - `LoraLoaderModelOnly` — `ln_lora`
  - `ModelSamplingSD3` — `ln_ms`
  - `KSamplerAdvanced` — `ln_ks`
- `VAEDecode` — `decode`
- `VHS_VideoCombine` — `save_video`

Required models/custom nodes:

- Wan 2.2 I2V high-noise GGUF:
  - `wan2.2_i2v_high_noise_14B_Q4_K_S.gguf`
- Wan 2.2 I2V low-noise GGUF:
  - `wan2.2_i2v_low_noise_14B_Q4_K_S.gguf`
- `wan_2.1_vae.safetensors`
- `umt5_xxl_fp8_e4m3fn_scaled.safetensors`
- `HearmemanAI_V4_Rank128_BreastsLoRA_Epoch80.safetensors`
- GGUF loader support, likely ComfyUI-GGUF
- Video Helper Suite for `VHS_VideoCombine`

Advantages:

- Genuine image-conditioned motion rather than two independently generated clips.
- High-noise and low-noise Wan stages are chained through the latent, improving temporal coherence.
- The source image conditions the initial video latent across the generated sequence.
- More suitable as a base for adding a multi-frame conditioning node than a simple clip-stitching workflow.

Limitations:

- Only one source image.
- No end-image input.
- No keyframe list, frame interpolation, or explicit first/last-frame conditioning.
- No latent continuity between separate generations.
- Text prompt controls motion; the source image primarily establishes appearance/composition.

Format:

- UI workflow only. It uses the ComfyUI graph format with `nodes`, `links`, widget values, and canvas positions.
- It is not API-workflow-compatible as-is because it lacks the API `class_type`/`inputs` prompt structure.
- The graph could be manually converted to an API prompt.

### 2. `the local vault/ComfyUI-Shared/user/default/workflows/I2V.json`

Second-best candidate, also single-image I2V.

Relevant nodes:

- `LoadImage` — ID `13`
  - Loads `nsfw_edit_00050_.png`.
- `ImageScaleToTotalPixels` — ID `22`
- `GetImageSize` — ID `21`
- `WanImageToVideo` — ID `14`
  - Receives the resized source through its `start_image` input, link `32`.
  - Width and height are derived from the source image.
  - No second image input exists.
- High-noise model path:
  - `UnetLoaderGGUF` — ID `1`
  - `LoraLoaderModelOnly` — IDs `3`, `5`
  - `ModelSamplingSD3` — ID `7`
  - `KSamplerAdvanced` — ID `15`, titled `KSampler HIGH (steps 0→10)`
- Low-noise model path:
  - `UnetLoaderGGUF` — ID `2`
  - `LoraLoaderModelOnly` — IDs `4`, `6`
  - `ModelSamplingSD3` — ID `8`
  - `KSamplerAdvanced` — ID `16`, titled `KSampler LOW (steps 10→20)`
- `VAEDecodeTiled` — ID `17`
- `VHS_VideoCombine` — ID `18`

Required models/custom nodes:

- `wan2.2_i2v_high_noise_14B_Q4_K_S.gguf`
- `wan2.2_i2v_low_noise_14B_Q4_K_S.gguf`
- `wan_2.1_vae.safetensors`
- `umt5_xxl_fp8_e4m3fn_scaled.safetensors`
- `Wan22_I2V_General_NSFW_HIGH_e8.safetensors`
- `Wan22_I2V_General_NSFW_LOW_e8.safetensors`
- `DR34ML4Y_I2V_14B_HIGH_V2.safetensors`
- `DR34ML4Y_I2V_14B_LOW_V2.safetensors`
- GGUF loader support
- Video Helper Suite
- `MathExpression|pysssss` and `INTConstant` nodes from auxiliary/custom node packs

Advantages:

- Genuine image-conditioned Wan 2.2 motion.
- Explicit high-noise/low-noise denoising split.
- Tiled VAE decoding is useful for larger outputs.
- More detailed model/LoRA experimentation than the other workflow.

Limitations:

- Only one input image via `start_image`.
- No end image or second keyframe.
- No interpolation/VFI nodes.
- No continuity mechanism for extending an existing clip.
- The workflow’s content-specific LoRAs make it less reusable.

Format:

- UI workflow only, not API prompt JSON.
- Requires conversion before use through an API endpoint.

## Explicit distinction

Neither candidate stitches two independently animated clips; both perform real single-image-to-video generation through `WanImageToVideo` and a shared latent denoising chain.

However, neither solves the requested two-image continuity problem. There are no nodes or connections for:

- `end_image`
- first/last-frame conditioning
- image batches used as temporal keyframes
- interpolation nodes such as RIFE or FILM
- latent blending between source images
- clip continuation or temporal context transfer

The remaining files are image, audio, or text-to-image workflows. `NSFW image editor 2.json` matched generic image-related searches but contains no video-generation or video-combine pipeline.

<response>
## Directly evidenced

- Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 officially accepts multiple images as an ordered list. Its example passes `[image1, image2]` with: “The magician bear is on the left, the alchemist bear is on the right…” [2511 model card](https://huggingface.co/Qwen/Qwen-Image-Edit-2511/blob/main/README.md#quick-start).
- The Diffusers implementation prefixes references in order as `Picture 1`, `Picture 2`, etc., and concatenates every image’s VAE latent. It defines no intrinsic roles such as “canvas,” “master,” or “identity reference”: [prompt construction](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/7685bffe89041496c2c0ae07ea933df1c80d1f43/src/diffusers/pipelines/qwenimage/pipeline_qwenimage_edit_plus.py#L228-L252), [latent concatenation](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/7685bffe89041496c2c0ae07ea933df1c80d1f43/src/diffusers/pipelines/qwenimage/pipeline_qwenimage_edit_plus.py#L445-L491).
- Qwen’s official prompt enhancer says prompts should be “direct and specific” and add only “minimal but sufficient details.” Clear instructions should retain their intent rather than be elaborated unnecessarily: [prompt_utils.py lines 181–198](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Image/blob/6b5e1f5cec987d404be5ac6657db3b9aacb56a89/src/examples/tools/prompt_utils.py#L181-L198). Qwen recommends this enhancer “for enhanced stability”: [README lines 324–330](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Image/blob/6b5e1f5cec987d404be5ac6657db3b9aacb56a89/README.md#L324-L330).
- For multi-image prompts, Qwen explicitly says to identify which picture supplies each element. Examples include “Change the girl in Picture 1 to the ink-wash style of Picture 2” and “Replace the girl of picture 1 with the boy of picture 2…”: [lines 218–232](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Image/blob/6b5e1f5cec987d404be5ac6657db3b9aacb56a89/src/examples/tools/prompt_utils.py#L218-L232). The latter’s “keeping picture 2’s background unchanged” is surprising if Picture 1 is intended as the canvas; use it as evidence for explicit role naming, not as a universally correct target/background recipe.
- Preservation should be scoped to the edit type. Qwen distinguishes:
 - low-level edits, where “all other regions…remain completely unchanged”;
 - high-level semantic edits, where overall pixels may change while semantic consistency is retained. 
 [Official Qwen blog](https://qwenlm.github.io/blog/qwen-image-edit/)
- For people, the official enhancer recommends naming preserved attributes and gives: “Replace the man’s hat with a dark brown beret; keep smile, short hair, and gray jacket unchanged”: [lines 207–213](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Image/blob/6b5e1f5cec987d404be5ac6657db3b9aacb56a89/src/examples/tools/prompt_utils.py#L207-L213).
- Qwen documents chained editing: repeatedly edit the previous result to correct localized errors. It does not document retaining the original as a second reference: [Qwen-Image-Edit.md lines 28–34](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Image/blob/6b5e1f5cec987d404be5ac6657db3b9aacb56a89/Qwen-Image-Edit.md#L28-L34).
- The reviewed first-party 2511 sources contain no validated prompt method for elapsed time, momentum, oscillation, continuous motion, or moving into/out of frame. The pipeline is a static image editor producing one image, not a temporal model.

## Evidence-aligned inference

- There is no official short-versus-long A/B result. However, “direct,” “specific,” and “minimal but sufficient” favors a short local delta plus a small invariant list over repeating a long scene bible every frame. Long prompts are not proven harmful; Diffusers defaults to 512 tokens and permits at most 1024: [pipeline source](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/7685bffe89041496c2c0ae07ea933df1c80d1f43/src/diffusers/pipelines/qwenimage/pipeline_qwenimage_edit_plus.py#L550-L576).
- Temporal language should be converted into a visible target state. For example: 
 `Picture 1 is the immediately previous frame. Move the runner one small step farther right, continuing the existing direction; right foot now forward, coat trailing left. Preserve identity, clothing, camera, lighting, background, and rendering style.` 
 For oscillation, state phase and direction—“moving left past center” or “at the rightmost extent beginning to reverse”—rather than relying only on “oscillating.”
- `Picture 1 = previous frame; Picture 2 = original master` is reasonable but unofficial. State both roles explicitly: 
 `Use Picture 1 for current pose, composition, and motion state. Use Picture 2 only to preserve face, hair, outfit, and proportions. Do not revert Picture 1’s evolved pose or position.` 
 Because both images enter conditioning and both VAE latents are concatenated, “only” is an instruction, not enforced isolation; Picture 2 may still pull composition toward the master.

## `TextEncodeQwenImageEditPlus_lrzjason`

At current commit `cdd4d02`, the source shows:

- Five image sockets; each present socket gets a `Picture N` marker.
- A system template asks the encoder to describe the images, interpret the edit, and maintain consistency.
- With a VAE, every image is encoded as a reference latent at approximately one megapixel, rounded to multiples of eight.
- By default, only Picture 1 is additionally resized to approximately `384×384` area for VL input. Pictures 2–5 remain approximately one megapixel. This contradicts the README’s broad statement that VL images are processed at 384.
- All reference latents are appended to conditioning.
- Its `LATENT` output is the first successfully encoded reference latent—normally Picture 1—not a model-defined “main image.”
- It contains no 2511-specific role logic.

Source: [nodes.py lines 209–333](https://github.com/lrzjason/Comfyui-QwenEditUtils/blob/cdd4d028c6491d27a40092d7795158668cec9189/nodes.py#L209-L333). For comparison, official ComfyUI resizes every VL input to approximately 384² and supports three images: [official node lines 53–105](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI/blob/5cc026f5b81b3f01fe7a1438a0fd4131d2ebda25/comfy_extras/nodes_qwen.py#L53-L105).

Therefore, Picture 1 behaves as the practical canvas only if the workflow feeds this node’s first-latent output into the sampler. The text encoder itself merely conditions on all supplied references.
</response>

  - low-level edits, where “all other regions…remain completely unchanged”;
  - high-level semantic edits, where overall pixels may change while semantic consistency is retained.  
  [Official Qwen blog](https://qwenlm.github.io/blog/qwen-image-edit/)
- For people, the official enhancer recommends naming preserved attributes and gives: “Replace the man’s hat with a dark brown beret; keep smile, short hair, and gray jacket unchanged”: [lines 207–213](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Image/blob/6b5e1f5cec987d404be5ac6657db3b9aacb56a89/src/examples/tools/prompt_utils.py#L207-L213).
- Qwen documents chained editing: repeatedly edit the previous result to correct localized errors. It does not document retaining the original as a second reference: [Qwen-Image-Edit.md lines 28–34](https://github.com/QwenLM/Qwen-Image/blob/6b5e1f5cec987d404be5ac6657db3b9aacb56a89/Qwen-Image-Edit.md#L28-L34).
- The reviewed first-party 2511 sources contain no validated prompt method for elapsed time, momentum, oscillation, continuous motion, or moving into/out of frame. The pipeline is a static image editor producing one image, not a temporal model.

## Evidence-aligned inference

- There is no official short-versus-long A/B result. However, “direct,” “specific,” and “minimal but sufficient” favors a short local delta plus a small invariant list over repeating a long scene bible every frame. Long prompts are not proven harmful; Diffusers defaults to 512 tokens and permits at most 1024: [pipeline source](https://github.com/huggingface/diffusers/blob/7685bffe89041496c2c0ae07ea933df1c80d1f43/src/diffusers/pipelines/qwenimage/pipeline_qwenimage_edit_plus.py#L550-L576).
- Temporal language should be converted into a visible target state. For example:  
  `Picture 1 is the immediately previous frame. Move the runner one small step farther right, continuing the existing direction; right foot now forward, coat trailing left. Preserve identity, clothing, camera, lighting, background, and rendering style.`  
  For oscillation, state phase and direction—“moving left past center” or “at the rightmost extent beginning to reverse”—rather than relying only on “oscillating.”
- `Picture 1 = previous frame; Picture 2 = original master` is reasonable but unofficial. State both roles explicitly:  
  `Use Picture 1 for current pose, composition, and motion state. Use Picture 2 only to preserve face, hair, outfit, and proportions. Do not revert Picture 1’s evolved pose or position.`  
  Because both images enter conditioning and both VAE latents are concatenated, “only” is an instruction, not enforced isolation; Picture 2 may still pull composition toward the master.

## `TextEncodeQwenImageEditPlus_lrzjason`

At current commit `cdd4d02`, the source shows:

- Five image sockets; each present socket gets a `Picture N` marker.
- A system template asks the encoder to describe the images, interpret the edit, and maintain consistency.
- With a VAE, every image is encoded as a reference latent at approximately one megapixel, rounded to multiples of eight.
- By default, only Picture 1 is additionally resized to approximately `384×384` area for VL input. Pictures 2–5 remain approximately one megapixel. This contradicts the README’s broad statement that VL images are processed at 384.
- All reference latents are appended to conditioning.
- Its `LATENT` output is the first successfully encoded reference latent—normally Picture 1—not a model-defined “main image.”
- It contains no 2511-specific role logic.

Source: [nodes.py lines 209–333](https://github.com/lrzjason/Comfyui-QwenEditUtils/blob/cdd4d028c6491d27a40092d7795158668cec9189/nodes.py#L209-L333). For comparison, official ComfyUI resizes every VL input to approximately 384² and supports three images: [official node lines 53–105](https://github.com/Comfy-Org/ComfyUI/blob/5cc026f5b81b3f01fe7a1438a0fd4131d2ebda25/comfy_extras/nodes_qwen.py#L53-L105).

Therefore, Picture 1 behaves as the practical canvas only if the workflow feeds this node’s first-latent output into the sampler. The text encoder itself merely conditions on all supplied references.

Inspected workflow `S9v0UpCVYcrtVJH4` read-only. It is active and named “PodCast Builder - for cursor - up to 6-frame FLF test.”

### 1. Node flow

Relevant path:

`Generate image`  
→ `Get image file`  
→ `Prepare first image for vision`  
→ `Analyze first image and plan second`  
→ `Parse second image plan`  
→ `Generate additional frames`  
→ `Drop Qwen image models`  
→ `Prepare frame downloads`  
→ `Get generated frame files`  
→ `Gather images`

Video path branches from generated frame downloads:

`Get generated frame files`  
→ `Prepare video render`  
→ `Generate video transitions`  
→ `Drop Wan video models`  
→ `Stitch video clips`  
→ `Get podcast video file`

Inputs to the planner include:

- `LLM config`: model, host, image count, execution/media ID
- `Parse audio prompt response`: storyboard/image prompt
- `Parse script response`: article summaries
- First generated Flux image, downloaded as binary and converted to base64

The workflow currently supports 2–6 images. Each additional image becomes the input for the next Qwen edit, creating a recursive frame chain.

### 2. Exact model settings and schemas

#### Analyze first image and plan second

HTTP POST:

```text
http://{llmHost}:11434/api/chat

Ollama settings:

  • model: gemma4:12b-it-qat
  • stream: false
  • keep_alive: 0
  • think: false
  • num_ctx: 8192
  • num_predict: 3000
  • temperature: 0.1
  • repeat_penalty: 1.1
  • HTTP timeout: 7,200,000 ms

The request uses a strict JSON schema with exactly these top-level fields:

  • actualSceneDescription: string
  • preservedElements: string[]
  • selectedStoryBeats: string[]
  • continuityStyle: string
  • motionTracks: object[]

Each motion track requires:

  • id
  • subject
  • mode: continuous | oscillating | finite
  • startFrame
  • endFrame
  • animatedAttributes: string[]
  • lockedAttributes: string[]
  • continuityDirective
  • frameStates: string[]

Additional properties are forbidden at both levels.

The prompt specifically requires:

  • 2–6 keyframes
  • roughly 2–3 motion tracks, maximum 6
  • explicit state for every frame
  • locked camera and scene continuity
  • no imageEditPrompts or transitionMotionPrompts in the model response
  • static, absolute frame descriptions rather than temporal wording
  • oscillating behavior for reversal, looping, pulsing, or return motion

Parse second image plan

The Code node:

  • Rejects Ollama done_reason === 'length'
  • Extracts JSON using a greedy object match
  • Requires at least one motion track
  • Clamps image count to 2–6
  • Normalizes missing fields and modes
  • Produces exactly imageCount - 1 image-edit prompts
  • Produces exactly imageCount - 1 transition-motion prompts
  • Preserves compatibility fields:
    • secondaryEditPrompt
    • tertiaryEditPrompt
    • transition1MotionPrompt
    • transition2MotionPrompt

It derives both prompt arrays from the same global motion plan, preventing image and video prompts from independently disagreeing.

Generate additional frames

ComfyUI workflow uses:

  • qwen-image-edit-2511-Q4_K_M.gguf
  • Qwen-Image-Edit-2511-Lightning-4steps-V1.0-bf16.safetensors
  • qwen_2.5_vl_7b_fp8_scaled.safetensors
  • qwen_image_vae.safetensors
  • 0.92 megapixel scaling
  • 4 Euler/simple sampling steps
  • CFG 1
  • denoise 1
  • same seed for all frame edits:
    abs(mediaRunId * 2654435761) % 4294967295
  • outputs named:
    cover_frame{N}_{mediaRunId}_00001_.png

Each frame is edited from the immediately preceding frame, not independently from the original.

Generate video transitions

Wan first/last-frame workflow uses:

  • wan_2.1_vae.safetensors
  • umt5_xxl_fp8_e4m3fn_scaled.safetensors
  • wan2.2_i2v_high_noise_14B_Q4_K_S.gguf
  • wan2.2_i2v_low_noise_14B_Q4_K_S.gguf
  • 29 latent frames
  • 16 fps
  • Euler/simple sampler
  • CFG 3.5
  • 8 total steps
  • high-noise pass: steps 0–5
  • low-noise pass: steps 5–8
  • H.264 MP4, CRF 19, YUV420p

3. Best insertion point for multi-stage deliberation

The safest seam is:

Prepare first image for vision
→ Analyze first image and plan second
→ [new deliberation stages]
→ Parse second image plan

Preserve the existing input contract to Parse second image plan: one JSON object containing the five planner fields, especially motionTracks.

A robust multi-stage design would be:

  1. Scene/identity extraction
  2. Story-beat selection
  3. Motion-track proposal
  4. Continuity/constraint critic
  5. Final plan synthesis

The final synthesis node should output the exact existing schema. The existing parser and all downstream nodes can remain unchanged.

Avoid inserting deliberation after Parse second image plan; by then the workflow has already materialized edit and transition prompts. Also avoid changing Generate additional frames, because it relies on the current prompt-array and compatibility-field contract.

A practical low-risk approach is to replace the single planner call with multiple sequential Ollama calls, passing compact JSON between them, and make the final call produce the current schema. This adds latency and token usage but minimizes downstream breakage.

4. Likely failure modes

  • Planner truncation: num_predict: 3000 may be insufficient for six frames and multiple tracks; the parser intentionally fails on done_reason: length.
  • Greedy JSON extraction: malformed or extra brace-containing text can cause incorrect extraction.
  • Schema drift: missing or renamed fields are partly normalized, but semantic errors remain possible.
  • Repeated frame states: the parser only appends a warning when states are identical; it does not truly validate physical progression.
  • Invalid motion semantics: no enforcement ensures continuous tracks are actually monotonic or oscillating tracks genuinely oscillate.
  • Track overlap ambiguity: multiple tracks can modify the same subject or attribute without conflict detection.
  • Prompt explosion: six frames and six tracks can produce very large edit and motion prompts.
  • Recursive drift: Qwen edits each prior generated frame, so identity, typography, geometry, and lighting errors can accumulate.
  • Single-seed correlation: all Qwen edits reuse one seed, potentially reinforcing artifacts across frames.
  • Filename assumptions: downstream nodes hardcode cover_frameN_{mediaRunId}_00001_.png; any ComfyUI naming variation breaks downloads.
  • Missing-frame handling: Get generated frame files does not visibly validate that every expected frame exists before video rendering.
  • Wan prompt mismatch: video rendering trusts generated transition prompts and does not compare actual frames against the declared motion plan.
  • Memory pressure: Qwen and Wan model unloading is sequential and dependent on successful upstream execution; failures may leave ComfyUI under memory pressure.
  • Input loss at merge points: Gather images and later merge nodes depend on item structure and branch ordering; unexpected item counts can silently affect media assembly.
  • Vision payload size: the first image is base64-encoded into the Ollama request, increasing request size and latency.
  • Storyboard inconsistency: Analyze first image and plan second receives both storyboard data and all summaries, so irrelevant summaries may dilute the selected visual story beats.

Raw excerpt 2 — assistant

  • bubbleId: 18d95ee9-c936-4209-b409-ec308a020841
  • createdAt: 2026-08-01T03:21:19.824Z
Use a staged planner/critic/compiler pipeline—not one agent asked to “think harder.” The LLM emits only compact, auditable scene facts; deterministic code compiles those facts into per-frame Qwen Image Edit requests.

## Pipeline

1. **Ingress + asset normalization**
   - Validate `start_image`, `end_image`, Wan settings, frame count, aspect ratio, policy/budget.
   - Store images privately; pass immutable URLs/keys plus SHA-256 hashes, never raw binary through agent tools.
   - Derive an idempotency key from image hashes + settings + prompt-template version.

2. **Pass A — visual inventory (vision LLM, structured output)**
   - Independently enumerate all visible entities in both endpoints.
   - Output concise evidence fields, not free-form reasoning.

3. **Pass B — correspondence and Wan motion plan (LLM)**
   - Match `start_id → end_id`; classify each entity as static, moving, appearing, disappearing, or occluded.
   - Specify camera motion, trajectories, pose/expression changes, occlusion order, and immutable identity anchors.

4. **Pass C — independent critic (LLM)**
   - Receives the inventory and proposed plan, but not the planner’s prose rationale.
   - Flags unsupported matches, impossible motion, static-element drift, endpoint contradictions, and likely Wan artifacts.

5. **Pass D — repair + final canonical plan (LLM)**
   - Revises only flagged fields; emits a final plan with stable IDs and a plan hash.
   - Require a high confidence score and zero blocking findings.

6. **Deterministic compiler (non-LLM)**
   - Interpolates each entity’s approved trajectory at frame `i / (N - 1)`.
   - Applies versioned prompt templates to produce Qwen Image Edit specs for every frame.
   - This is what makes per-frame output reproducible: temperature-zero LLM output alone is not a determinism guarantee.

7. **Qwen edit execution → Wan render**
   - Submit approved per-frame specs with bounded concurrency.
   - Validate first/last generated frames against the approved endpoint constraints before submitting to Wan.

## Core contracts

```ts
type SceneElement = {
  id: string;                         // stable: "subject.primary", "prop.mug"
  kind: "person" | "animal" | "object" | "background" | "effect";
  start: { visible: boolean; anchors: string[]; state: Record<string, string> };
  end:   { visible: boolean; anchors: string[]; state: Record<string, string> };
  role: "static" | "moving" | "appears" | "disappears" | "occluded";
  evidence: string[];                 // observable facts only
  confidence: number;                 // 0..1
};

type MotionPlan = {
  camera: { motion: "locked" | "pan" | "tilt" | "push" | "pull"; intensity: 0 | 1 | 2 };
  elements: Array<{
    id: string;
    correspondence: string | null;
    trajectory: "hold" | "linear" | "arc" | "turn" | "enter" | "exit";
    timing: [number, number];         // normalized 0..1
    easing: "linear" | "ease-in" | "ease-out" | "ease-in-out";
    preserve: string[];               // identity/wardrobe/background anchors
  }>;
};

type FrameEditSpec = {
  job_id: string;
  plan_hash: string;
  frame_index: number;
  t: number;
  source_asset_key: string;
  qwen: {
    prompt: string;
    negative_prompt: string;
    strength: number;
    seed: number;
    preserve: string[];
  };
  expected: { visible_ids: string[]; camera: string };
};

Validation gates

Gate Reject when
Input hashes/URLs missing, incompatible dimensions, unsupported frame count
Inventory duplicate IDs, unclassified visible object, low-confidence primary subject
Correspondence a primary subject has no start/end match without an explicit appear/disappear rule
Motion a static element changes; motion timing is outside [0,1]; camera plan conflicts with endpoint framing
Critique any blocking issue remains, or endpoint similarity is below threshold
Compilation non-contiguous frame indices, missing seed/template version, prompt exceeds provider limits
Render preflight generated endpoint violates identity anchors or differs materially from approved endpoint

Keep a “semantic diff” check between final plan and critic-approved plan: only critic-authorized fields may change during repair.

n8n shape

Use Basic LLM Chain + structured output parser for each pass, rather than a tool-using Agent. This is a stateless, fixed sequence and is easier to audit.

Webhook → Validate → Stage assets → Inventory → Correspondence/Motion → Critic → Repair → Deterministic compiler → Qwen queue → Endpoint QA → Wan submit → Respond

  • Persist plans, critiques, prompt-template version, hashes, and provider request IDs in durable storage.
  • Put secrets in n8n credentials; use private object-storage references for images.
  • Configure retries for provider calls (maxTries: 3, 5-second waits), explicit error outputs, and a workflow-level error workflow.
  • n8n fan-out is sequential; do not assume per-frame edits run in parallel. Use a rate-limited external queue/worker or asynchronous sub-workflow dispatch only if Qwen quotas permit it.

Cost and latency

For N frames:

  • LLM planning cost: 4 multimodal/structured calls: inventory, plan, critic, repair.
  • Generation cost: N Qwen edits plus one Wan render; this dominates at moderate/high N.
  • Latency: planning calls are intentionally serial; then generation is approximately N / concurrency provider batches. Cap concurrency conservatively to avoid 429s and inconsistent retries.
  • Cache by the idempotency key. Reuse the canonical plan when only rendering is retried; do not re-plan unless inputs or templates changed.

Avoid hidden chain-of-thought

Do not prompt: “reason step by step,” “show all reasoning,” or “internally enumerate everything before answering.” Those do not reliably improve quality and invite disclosure of private reasoning.

Instead require observable, bounded artifacts:

  • SceneElement[] with evidence strings,
  • explicit correspondence edges,
  • normalized trajectories,
  • machine-readable critique findings,
  • repair diffs.

The critic judges the plan from those artifacts, and deterministic validation enforces their invariants. This produces inspectable deliberation without depending on or collecting hidden chain-of-thought.

# Executive conclusion

As of 2026-08-01, there is no production-ready local stack that combines all of these on a 36GB M3 Mac:

1. multiple hard keyframes,
2. genuine multi-frame motion inheritance,
3. high-quality Wan-class output,
4. reliable Apple Silicon acceleration,
5. reasonable render time.

The best technical design is Wan 2.2 + SVI 2.0 Pro latent continuation, augmented with `ComfyUI-Wan-SVI2Pro-FLF` for endpoint control. It carries the previous segment’s native latent tail into the next segment, avoiding decode/re-encode loss. But it requires two 14B Wan 2.2 experts and two SVI LoRAs; full precision does not fit comfortably in 36GB, FP8 is not natively supported by MPS, and quantized ComfyUI operation is slow and fragile.

My concrete recommendation:

1. Best practical local prototype: Wan2.1-VACE-1.3B at 480p, using 8–16 real overlap frames and positioned endpoint references. It fits the Mac much more realistically, but its continuation is control-video/pixel-conditioned rather than native latent continuation.
2. Best local fidelity experiment: Wan 2.2 SVI 2.0 Pro + FLF, quantized to Q2/Q3, 480p, initially 41 frames, `motion_latent_count=1`, SDPA attention, and aggressive sequential unloading. Expect long runtimes and possible MPS incompatibilities.
3. Best paid proof baseline: official hosted Wan 2.7 continuation, with the previous clip as `first_clip` and the next keyframe as optional `last_frame`. This directly tests whether the local methods are losing motion continuity or merely hitting model limits.
4. Best Mac-native engine if strict continuation is relaxed: MLX-Video with Wan 2.2 or LTX-2.3. It is substantially better matched to Apple hardware, but its published interface does not currently expose SVI `prev_samples`, VACE, or LTX keyframe-interpolation pipelines.

“Velocity inheritance” needs one qualification: none of these systems exposes a physical velocity vector. SVI carries a learned temporal latent containing local motion state; VACE and hosted continuation infer velocity from several input frames. SVI is therefore the closest match to the requested property, but not an explicit physics representation.

# 1. Wan SVI / SVI 2.0 Pro

## What SVI Pro actually carries forward

**Sourced fact:** SVI 2.0 Pro builds each new conditioning sequence as:

```text
[anchor latent, previous clip motion latent, zero-valued latent padding]

It never decodes the previous last frame and re-encodes it for continuation. This is the central advantage over frame-chaining: no VAE round trip at every segment boundary.

Primary sources:

  • SVI 2.0 Pro design note
  • Exact pipeline implementation
  • Official Wan 2.2 SVI branch
  • SVI paper

The paper reports only a 0.63% subject-consistency drop in its ultra-long evaluation, versus 7.03% for ordinary Wan 2.1 and 13.71% for FramePack. That result is from the authors’ benchmark and hardware, not a guarantee for quantized ComfyUI output.

Exact models and LoRAs

For Wan 2.2 SVI 2.0 Pro:

  • Base model: Wan2.2-I2V-A14B
  • high-noise expert: early denoising/layout/motion
  • low-noise expert: later detail refinement
  • Official SVI Pro high-noise LoRA:
  • SVI_Wan2.2-I2V-A14B_high_noise_lora_v2.0_pro.safetensors
  • Official SVI Pro low-noise LoRA:
  • SVI_Wan2.2-I2V-A14B_low_noise_lora_v2.0_pro.safetensors
  • Official model directory:
  • vita-video-gen/svi-model/version-2.0
  • Comfy-native converted versions:
  • SVI_v2_PRO_Wan2.2-I2V-A14B_HIGH_lora_rank_128_fp16.safetensors
  • SVI_v2_PRO_Wan2.2-I2V-A14B_LOW_lora_rank_128_fp16.safetensors
  • Kijai converted SVI directory

Load each SVI LoRA only into its matching high- or low-noise expert.

For Wan 2.1:

  • SVI_Wan2.1-I2V-14B_lora_v2.0.safetensors
  • This is SVI 2.0, not the same latent-continuation Pro architecture.
  • The authors explicitly warn that it cannot use an ordinary Wan 2.1 workflow because it needs modified padding.

Official baseline settings

The official Wan 2.2 example uses:

  • 832×480
  • 81 frames per clip
  • 15 fps
  • num_motion_latent=1
  • num_overlap_frame=5
  • different seed per clip
  • 50 clips in the published long-run command

Source: SVI Wan 2.2 README.

The official script uses:

seed = clip_idx * seed_multiplier
prev_last_latent = generated latent tail
next clip = video_frames[num_overlap_frame:]

Source: inference_svi_2.0_pro.py.

prev_samples and motion_latent_count

In the Comfy implementation:

  • prev_samples must be the sampler’s native output latent, shaped [B,C,T,H,W].
  • motion_latent_count=1 copies its final temporal slot.
  • motion_latent_count=2 copies two temporal slots.
  • 0 disables temporal continuation.

Because Wan has temporal stride 4, one latent slot spans approximately four new frames, with boundary accounting making the practical overlap five decoded frames.

Recommendation: start with 1. It is the official Pro setting and leaves the model more freedom to reach the next keyframe. Test 2 only for rapid or strongly directional motion; it can preserve more local trajectory but may also echo poses, overconstrain the beginning, or fight endpoint guidance.

Never decode and re-encode the previous clip to construct prev_samples; that removes the main benefit of SVI Pro.

2. ComfyUI-Wan-SVI2Pro-FLF

Repository: Well-Made/ComfyUI-Wan-SVI2Pro-FLF

Exact nodes

The package adds:

  • WanImageToVideoSVIProFLF
  • category: conditioning/video_models
  • WanCutLastSlot
  • category: latent/video

Its supplied workflows use either:

  • KSampler (Advanced), or
  • SamplerCustomAdvanced

and use Image Batch Extend With Overlap for decoded-frame assembly.

The normal upstream node is:

  • WanImageToVideoSVIPro

from ComfyUI-KJNodes, with anchor_samples, optional prev_samples, and motion_latent_count.

For model loading, retain the official native Wan 2.2 I2V dual-expert template and load the SVI high/low LoRAs into their corresponding experts. The FLF node replaces the ordinary image-to-video conditioning stage; it does not replace Wan’s high/low sampler architecture.

Endpoint handling

The FLF node constructs:

anchor_samples
+ last motion_latent_count slots from prev_samples
+ Wan-format zero padding

It then overwrites the final temporal slots with end_samples and sets those slots to zero in concat_mask. In this mask convention, zero means the corresponding conditioning latent is hard-locked.

Source code: nodes.py.

This is an experimental composition of two independently useful mechanisms:

  • SVI motion continuation at the start;
  • FLF hard endpoint control at the end.

It is not an officially trained SVI endpoint mode.

Why the last-slot cut exists

A hard endpoint can conflict with SVI’s learned motion trajectory. The repository documents “crumpled” or heavily distorted frames when the final hard-locked latent is fed back as the next clip’s motion context.

The recommended workaround is:

generated latent
 ├─ decode full latent for output
 └─ WanCutLastSlot(slots_to_cut=1) → next segment prev_samples

This preserves the visible endpoint in the assembled video but prevents the exact hard-locked terminal slot from steering the next generation.

Recommendation: use this split-path design. Do not trim the only copy before decoding.

Repository caveats

The node is useful, but not yet production-hardened:

  • Its schema declares prev_samples as required although the implementation and README describe it as optional for the first segment.
  • VAE chunk boundaries can vary enough that the repository recommends adjusting decoded overlap by one or two frames.
  • The author says compatibility with arbitrary model combinations is not exhaustively tested.
  • The repository notes washed-out output and includes a contrast-adjustment workaround.
  • Its endpoint mechanism can reduce prompt adherence when the segment is too short.

These are reasons to treat FLF as an experiment requiring QA, not a drop-in deterministic animation solver.

3. Recommended SVI multi-keyframe graph

Given keyframes K0 … Kn:

Segment 0

  • anchor_samples = VAE(K0)
  • end_samples = VAE(K1)
  • no meaningful previous latent
  • motion_latent_count = 0
  • generate 81 frames initially

Because of the current required-input declaration, the provided workflow may need an anchor/repeated latent connected to prev_samples, or the first segment may use ordinary FLF conditioning before switching to the SVI-FLF node.

Segment i > 0

  • anchor_samples = VAE(Ki)
  • prev_samples = WanCutLastSlot(previous raw generated latent, 1)
  • end_samples = VAE(Ki+1)
  • motion_latent_count = 1
  • use a new seed
  • keep subject/style text stable while changing only action and camera direction

Stitching

  • Keep all frames from segment 0.
  • Remove the first five decoded frames from each subsequent segment, matching the official SVI configuration.
  • If ghosting remains, test 4, 5, and 6—not arbitrary large overlaps.
  • Prefer a hard overlap removal over a long dissolve. Crossfades often create double limbs and reduce apparent velocity.
  • If a blend is necessary, align the overlap with optical flow first and blend only one or two frames.

The FLF repository’s adjustable overlap addresses VAE boundary variation. The official SVI five-frame trim remains the principled starting point.

Segment duration

Use 81 frames for initial tests. The FLF author reports that 81–101 frames can improve prompt adherence because the beginning is occupied with continuing previous motion and the end is occupied with endpoint convergence.

For hard keyframes that imply a major pose or camera change, give the model more temporal room rather than increasing endpoint strength.

4. Wan 2.1 VACE continuation

Primary implementation: ali-vilab/VACE

Official variants

  • Wan2.1-VACE-1.3B
  • approximately 81×480×832
  • Wan2.1-VACE-14B
  • approximately 81×720×1280
  • VACE-LTX-Video-0.9
  • approximately 97×512×768

The official code was tested with CUDA 12.4 and PyTorch 2.5.1. It does not claim native MPS support.

How VACE continuation works

VACE accepts:

  • src_video
  • src_mask
  • reference images
  • prompt

For temporal continuation, a source/control video shorter than the requested output is treated as temporal outpainting. Sliding-window implementations preserve overlap from the previous window and generate the remainder.

Useful control representation:

  • black mask: preserve
  • white mask: process
  • grey value 127 in the control video: regenerate/inpaint
  • positioned reference images: force a particular image near a chosen frame

Source:

  • VACE README
  • VACE User Guide
  • Wan2GP VACE guide
  • Wan2GP temporal-processing guide

Practical multi-keyframe recipe

For each segment:

  1. Carry the final 8–16 real frames from the previous segment into the new control video.
  2. Mark those frames “keep unchanged.”
  3. Fill the future region with VACE’s regeneration/inpainting representation.
  4. Position the next keyframe at the final desired frame.
  5. Generate only a short window.
  6. Remove the duplicated overlap from the output.
  7. Persist each completed segment to disk before starting the next.

The contiguous overlap provides enough observations for VACE to infer direction and approximate speed. It is more informative than last-frame chaining but still incurs VAE/control conditioning and may alter the preserved area slightly.

Memory variants and optimization

Recommendation for this Mac: start with the 1.3B model at 480p. It is the only official VACE variant with a realistic memory margin.

For 14B:

  • quantization is effectively mandatory;
  • block swapping on a Mac does not create more physical memory because CPU and GPU share the same unified pool;
  • it may reduce MPS-private allocations, but every copied/offloaded block still occupies the same 36GB and adds synchronization overhead.

Disk-backed segment storage and incremental assembly prevent long videos from filling RAM. Community implementations such as wan-video-extender and ComfyUI_vaceFramepack offer such mechanisms, but their “arbitrary length” and semantic-memory selectors are community additions, not official VACE guarantees.

VACE is the more practical Mac choice; SVI Pro remains the cleaner motion-continuation architecture.

5. Hosted Wan 2.7 baseline

As of the access date, I found official hosted Wan 2.7 APIs but no official downloadable Wan 2.7 weights or local inference repository. Treat claims that Wan 2.7 is currently open-weight/local as unverified unless Alibaba publishes those assets.

Official model: wan2.7-i2v-2026-04-25

The API supports:

  • first-frame-to-video;
  • first-and-last-frame-to-video;
  • video continuation;
  • first_clip plus optional last_frame;
  • 720p or 1080p;
  • total duration 2–15 seconds.

In continuation mode, the returned video includes the original input clip. If a two-second source is submitted with duration 12, the result is two seconds of original footage plus ten generated seconds.

Primary sources:

  • Wan 2.7 I2V API
  • Wan 2.7 I2V guide
  • Alibaba Model Studio pricing

International pricing on 2026-08-01:

  • 720p: $0.10 per output second
  • 1080p: $0.15 per output second
  • initial 50-second quota listed by Alibaba
  • failed requests are not billed
  • input is free, but continuation’s returned total duration includes the input clip

Thus a 12-second continuation containing a two-second input is billed for 12 seconds, not only the ten generated seconds.

fal.ai also lists $0.10/output-second for its Wan 2.7 endpoints: fal Wan 2.7.

Baseline protocol

For every difficult local segment:

  1. Submit the local previous clip, not merely its last frame.
  2. Supply the same target endpoint as last_frame.
  3. Use the same action/camera prompt.
  4. Compare:
  • seam velocity;
  • endpoint adherence;
  • identity retention;
  • prompt compliance;
  • motion amplitude.

If Wan 2.7 succeeds and local VACE/SVI fails, the problem is likely local model capacity or quantization. If Wan 2.7 also fails, the keyframe transition itself may be underdetermined or physically implausible.

6. Other local and long-video systems

LTX-Video / LTX-2 / LTX-2.3

Official code: Lightricks/LTX-2

Current LTX-2.3 provides:

  • 22B dev and distilled models;
  • synchronized audio/video;
  • KeyframeInterpolationPipeline;
  • image-to-video;
  • video-to-video via IC-LoRA;
  • retake of a selected temporal region;
  • an eight-step distilled pipeline;
  • CPU/disk offload;
  • FP8 quantization.

This is arguably the strongest open multi-keyframe toolkit by feature breadth. But the official acceleration path targets CUDA, FlashAttention 3/4, and FP8. A 22B BF16 transformer alone is around 44GB before text encoder, VAE, audio model, and activations.

The official Comfy package is Lightricks/ComfyUI-LTXVideo. Open issues document CUDA prerequisites and MPS failures.

Mac-native alternatives exist:

  • Blaizzy/mlx-video
  • dgrauet/ltx-2-mlx

These support quantized LTX-2.3 T2V/I2V/A2V much more naturally on Apple Silicon. However, their documented interfaces do not currently expose the official keyframe interpolation, retake, or native continuation pipelines. Therefore LTX is promising but does not presently beat SVI/VACE for this exact local task.

FramePack / FramePack-F1

Official repository: lllyasviel/FramePack

Strengths:

  • genuine next-section prediction;
  • constant-length packed context;
  • workload approximately invariant with video duration;
  • F1 predicts only forward from history and has greater dynamics;
  • official claim: 13B model can generate one minute using 6GB NVIDIA VRAM.

Limits:

  • officially requires NVIDIA RTX, Linux or Windows;
  • no official macOS/MPS support;
  • not designed around arbitrary hard intermediate keyframes;
  • TeaCache, quantization, and alternate attention can materially change results;
  • its 1.5–2.5 seconds/frame figures are RTX 4090 figures, not Mac estimates.

FramePack is an excellent long free-running motion model but not a viable official M3 method and not a deterministic keyframe path solver.

SkyReels-V2 Diffusion Forcing

Official repository: SkyworkAI/SkyReels-V2

This is a true autoregressive/diffusion-forcing long-video system:

  • continuation from preceding frames;
  • video extension;
  • start/end frame control;
  • synchronous and asynchronous modes;
  • cleaner earlier blocks condition noisier later blocks.

Official peak figures:

  • 1.3B 540p: approximately 14.7GB
  • 14B 540p: approximately 51.2GB
  • ordinary 14B I2V path: approximately 43.4GB

The inference code moves pipelines to CUDA explicitly. It is theoretically small enough in its 1.3B form, but not a supported MPS solution.

SkyReels-V3

Official repository: SkyworkAI/SkyReels-V3

This supersedes V2 for several production uses:

  • dedicated 14B 720p video-extension model;
  • single-shot continuation from 5–30 seconds;
  • shot-switching continuation;
  • reference-to-video;
  • FP8 weight-only low-VRAM mode plus block offload.

It recommends CUDA 12.8. Its low-VRAM path depends on FP8 and block offload, making it unsuitable for this Mac despite being one of the stronger current open continuation systems.

HunyuanVideo

Original HunyuanVideo requires NVIDIA CUDA and officially lists roughly 45–60GB minimum depending on output size: Tencent-Hunyuan/HunyuanVideo.

HunyuanVideo-1.5 is much more efficient:

  • 8.3B parameters;
  • T2V and I2V;
  • 480p distilled I2V at 8 or 12 steps;
  • 13.6GB peak for 720p/121 frames in the authors’ CUDA pipeline with pipeline/group offload and VAE tiling.

It still lacks native arbitrary multi-keyframe continuation. Last-frame chaining discards velocity, so it is not a preferred solution here.

CogVideoX

Official repository: zai-org/CogVideo

CogVideoX offers:

  • 2B and 5B variants;
  • sequential CPU offload;
  • INT8/FP8 examples;
  • DDIM inversion;
  • a separate CogVideoX-Interpolation project.

It is lighter and older, but neither its mainline model nor the interpolation fork offers a better combination of motion continuation, keyframe control, quality, and Apple support than VACE or LTX.

LongCat-Video

Official repository: meituan-longcat/LongCat-Video

This is a serious current alternative:

  • 13.6B;
  • native T2V, I2V, and video continuation in one model;
  • trained for minute-long continuation;
  • claims no color drift or quality degradation;
  • explicit run_demo_video_continuation.py and long-video scripts.

Its official stack requires CUDA, FlashAttention, and usually torch.compile; it is not a Mac solution.

Newer research-only systems

  • NVIDIA LongLive: native long-video autoregression with KV recaching and frame sinks, up to 240 seconds. Official requirement is Linux/NVIDIA with at least 40GB.
  • Helios/Open-Sora-Plan: minute-scale long generation at 19.5 FPS on one H100, not a Mac implementation.
  • LongLive 2.0: stronger 5B long generation using NVFP4 and Blackwell-specific infrastructure, fundamentally unavailable on M3.
  • DreaMontage paper: arbitrary-frame and multi-keyframe conditioning is highly relevant, but it is presently a research result rather than a mature local Mac workflow.

7. Apple Silicon reality

MPS

PyTorch’s MPS backend provides GPU access through Metal and shares unified memory with the CPU:

  • PyTorch MPS documentation
  • PyTorch Apple Silicon architecture overview

Unified memory avoids PCIe copies but does not make all 36GB safely available to a model. macOS, display buffers, Python, ComfyUI, decoded frames, model weights, activations, and temporary VAE tensors share it.

FP8

MPS does not natively support the FP8 workflow assumed by many Wan and LTX templates. A documented Wan 2.2 ComfyUI failure is:

Trying to convert Float8_e4m3fn to the MPS backend but it does not have support for that dtype.

Source: ComfyUI issue #9255.

Experimental compatibility shims exist, such as ComfyUI-AppleSilicon-FP8, but this is not native FP8 execution. It routes conversions or substitutes Metal kernels and explicitly describes some paths as experimental.

GGUF

GGUF Q2/Q3 makes dual-14B Wan 2.2 physically loadable, but:

  • low-bit dequantization can be slow;
  • LoRA application can increase working memory;
  • VAE decoding can still OOM independently;
  • Q2 may damage motion/detail enough to compromise the test.

A community report on an M3 Max 36GB measured about 700 seconds for 41 Wan 2.2 frames using Q2, while 81 frames caused VAE memory failure. That is anecdotal rather than an official benchmark, but it is consistent with the expected memory boundary.

MLX

MLX is the better Apple-native execution layer. mlx-video supports:

  • Wan 2.1/2.2;
  • LTX-2/2.3;
  • quantized weights;
  • Wan 2.2 high/low LoRAs;
  • four-step Wan2.2-Lightning.

Its present missing feature is the conditioning interface needed for this task: SVI prev_samples, FLF endpoints, VACE temporal outpainting, or LTX keyframe interpolation.

A future MLX port of the SVI conditioning formula would likely be the best M3 solution, because the algorithm itself is simple compared with porting the full model. It is not currently an off-the-shelf method.

8. Acceleration compatibility

SVI

SVI is not a speed accelerator. It is a continuation/error-recycling LoRA and conditioning design. Normal denoising cost remains.

LightX2V / Wan2.2-Lightning

Official sources:

  • ModelTC/LightX2V
  • ModelTC/Wan2.2-Lightning
  • Wan2.2 Distill LoRAs

Wan 2.2 I2V requires matching high- and low-noise distillation LoRAs. Four total steps can work, though more often improves quality.

SVI Pro’s anchor redesign was explicitly intended to alleviate conflict with LightX2V. That does not mean every LightX2V version is validated. The SVI team still advises reducing LightX2V use when motion becomes slow and using 480p. Community tests report better long-run color stability with the Wan 2.2-specific LoRAs than using Wan 2.1 480p LoRAs at 720p.

Recommendation: establish the non-accelerated SVI result first. Then add one matched Wan 2.2 LightX2V high/low pair. Do not simultaneously add Lightning, CausVid, TeaCache, and alternate attention because the failure source becomes unknowable.

CausVid

Primary project: tianweiy/CausVid

Available Wan LoRAs are primarily based on Wan 2.1 T2V. They can reduce generation to roughly 4–12 steps, but are not an officially supported pair for Wan 2.2 SVI Pro’s two I2V experts.

Do not use a Wan2.1 CausVid LoRA as the primary SVI Pro accelerator unless accepting an unsupported experiment. It may weaken image/keyframe adherence and motion amplitude.

Attention and caching

Use PyTorch SDPA on the Mac.

Avoid assuming that SageAttention, FlashAttention, or TeaCache are lossless:

  • FlashAttention is CUDA-targeted.
  • SageAttention has community reports of SVI seam flashing.
  • FramePack’s author explicitly shows that TeaCache and quantization can materially alter outputs.

For final QA runs, disable cache approximations.

9. Concrete local test plan

Phase A: practical VACE baseline

  • Wan2.1-VACE-1.3B
  • 832×480
  • 41 frames first, then 81 if stable
  • FP16/BF16, not FP8
  • SDPA
  • 8 real overlap frames initially
  • next keyframe positioned at final frame
  • original VACE: 15–30 steps
  • disk-save each segment immediately

Test overlap values 5, 8, 12, and 16. Choose the smallest that preserves velocity without propagating blur.

Phase B: SVI Pro feasibility

  • Wan 2.2 I2V high/low Q2 or Q3 GGUF
  • matching SVI Pro high/low FP16 LoRAs
  • WanImageToVideoSVIProFLF
  • WanCutLastSlot(1)
  • 480p
  • 41 frames
  • motion_latent_count=1
  • five-frame decoded overlap trim
  • SDPA
  • unique seed per segment
  • no acceleration LoRA initially

If stable:

  1. increase to 81 frames;
  2. test motion_latent_count=2;
  3. test one matched LightX2V high/low pair;
  4. only then test longer sequences.

Phase C: hosted control

Run the same transition through Wan 2.7 at 720p using:

first_clip = preceding segment
last_frame = next keyframe
duration = input duration + intended continuation

Do not compare a local 480p Q2 output against Wan 2.7 solely on sharpness. Compare motion continuity and endpoint achievement separately.

10. Stitching and QA

Seam mechanics

For each seam retain:

  • the previous segment’s last 12–16 frames;
  • the next segment’s first 12–16 frames;
  • raw latents where available;
  • the exact overlap removed;
  • seed, prompt, model, LoRAs, and quantization.

Perform assembly in this order:

  1. remove deterministic duplicated overlap;
  2. inspect seam at full speed;
  3. inspect frame-by-frame;
  4. try ±1 frame trim;
  5. color-match only after temporal alignment;
  6. use optical-flow blending only as a last resort.

Recommended metrics

Primary evaluation suites:

  • VBench
  • EvalCrafter paper

Track:

  • subject consistency;
  • background consistency;
  • temporal flicker;
  • motion smoothness;
  • dynamic degree;
  • prompt/action consistency.

Add seam-specific measurements:

  1. Velocity jump Estimate optical flow before and after the seam. Compare median magnitude and direction. Normalize against ordinary within-segment variation.

  2. Seam warping error Warp the final pre-seam frame toward the first post-seam frame using optical flow and measure residual error.

  3. Keyframe adherence Compare generated endpoint against the requested keyframe using LPIPS plus DINO/CLIP similarity. Pixel SSIM alone over-penalizes valid texture changes.

  4. Identity drift DINO or face-embedding similarity from the original anchor to every segment endpoint.

  5. Color drift Compare Lab histogram/Delta-E across segment interiors and seams.

  6. Motion-collapse check Always report dynamic degree alongside consistency. A nearly static video can score deceptively well on flicker and identity.

  7. Human review Loop each seam three times at normal speed, then half speed. Rate:

  • trajectory continuity;
  • body/object deformation;
  • camera acceleration;
  • endpoint naturalness;
  • visible pause or reset.

Use relative acceptance thresholds: seam errors should fall within the median plus two standard deviations of ordinary internal frame transitions. This adapts to the motion intensity of each shot better than a universal LPIPS or flow cutoff.

Final recommendation

For this exact M3/36GB machine:

  • Use VACE 1.3B for a workflow you can realistically iterate locally.
  • Use SVI 2.0 Pro + FLF only as the high-value latent-continuation experiment, at 480p/Q2–Q3 and short windows.
  • Do not rely on FP8, block swap, or CUDA-specific attention to rescue the 14B stack on MPS.
  • Prefer MLX for ordinary Wan/LTX generation, but it does not yet expose the required continuation/keyframe controls.
  • Keep Wan 2.7 continuation as the paid reference implementation.
  • If the project becomes production-critical, an NVIDIA machine with at least 24GB VRAM—or rented 48GB+ GPU—is materially more suitable than the M3 Mac for SVI Pro, SkyReels V3, LongCat, or full LTX keyframe interpolation.
